lessons.title: Predict and Observe: Elastic vs Plastic Behaviour — The Kericho Bridge Rope Mystery

quiz.prompt: In the Kericho story, an 80 kg sack of tea leaves is placed on a footbridge held by two sisal ropes, Rope A and Rope B. Which statement correctly describes what was observed?
choices: Rope A stretched and returned to its original length when the load was removed, while Rope B stretched and then snapped.
Rope A snapped straight away, while Rope B stretched and returned to its original length.
Both ropes stretched and returned to their original length, but Rope B was slower.
Neither rope changed length, but Rope B snapped when the sack was added.
quiz.rationale: The story shows Rope A stretching and springing back, and Rope B stretching permanently and then snapping. The question checks only what was observed.
quiz.placement: Predict: teacher-narrated Kericho bridge story with projected photographs

quiz.prompt: After the sticky-note predictions are put on the board, the teacher does not say which ones are right. What is the best way to think about these predictions at this stage?
choices: They are first ideas to be tested with evidence later, so some may need to change.
They are final answers, because every learner wrote one.
They are correct only if most of the class wrote the same idea.
They are wrong, because the teacher did not confirm them.
quiz.rationale: Predictions are first guesses made before evidence is collected. The class holds all ideas and tests them as the unit goes on.
quiz.placement: Predict: sticky-note predictions and teacher clustering of ideas on the board

quiz.prompt: A group hangs masses from a 15 cm piece of copper wire, then removes all the masses. The wire stays bent and does not return to its original shape. Using the activity card, how should the group classify the copper wire?
choices: Plastic, because it did not return to its original shape when the load was removed
Elastic, because the wire did not break
Fractured, because any change in shape counts as breaking
Elastic, because it changed shape when the masses were added
quiz.rationale: The test for elastic behaviour is whether the material returns to its original shape after unloading. The wire did not, so it is plastic. Bending under load alone does not make a material elastic.
quiz.placement: Observe: hands-on exploration with rubber band, sisal twine and copper wire, two-column table

quiz.prompt: A group records the length of a piece of sisal twine in its two-column table. Resting length: 15.0 cm. Length while holding 200 g: 16.5 cm. Length after all masses are removed: 16.2 cm. By how much is the twine permanently longer than its resting length?
choices: 1.2 cm
0.3 cm
1.5 cm
quiz.rationale: Permanent change is the length after unloading minus the resting length: 16.2 − 15.0 = 1.2 cm. This twine did not return to its original length, so it shows plastic behaviour.
quiz.placement: Observe: recording 'What happened when unloaded' in the two-column table

quiz.prompt: During the activity, one material stretches as masses are added and then snaps into two pieces before 200 g is reached. Which category on the activity card (elastic, plastic or fractured) fits it best?
choices: Elastic, because it stretched at first
Fractured, because it broke under the load
Plastic, because it is still in one piece but permanently longer
Unchanged, because it did not return to its original length
quiz.rationale: A material that breaks apart under the load is classified as fractured. It cannot be called elastic because it did not return to its original length.
quiz.placement: Observe: classifying each material as elastic, plastic or fractured

quiz.prompt: A learner says: 'Rope B snapped because it was older, so we already know the reason.' Which response is best at this point in the unit?
choices: The reason has not been explained yet. Age is one idea to test with evidence in later lessons.
The learner is right, because Rope B was thinner than Rope A.
The learner is right, because older things are always weaker.
The learner is wrong, because age never affects a rope.
quiz.rationale: The lesson leaves the puzzle open. Age was only one of the learners' ideas, and the class will test such ideas in later lessons rather than accept them now.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: posting yellow and pink sticky-note questions about why the ropes behaved differently

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly describes elastic behaviour of a material?
choices: The material breaks when a force is applied.
The material stretches a very large amount.
The material returns to its original shape and size when the force is removed.
The material bends and stays bent after the force is removed.
quiz.rationale: Elastic behaviour means the material returns to its original shape and size after the force is removed. Stretchiness alone is not enough.
quiz.placement: Explain: mini-explanation introducing the terms elastic behaviour and plastic deformation

lessons.title: Stretching the Truth: Elastic vs. Plastic Behaviour in Real Materials

quiz.prompt: A group hangs a rubber band from a clamp. Its original length is 20 cm. With a 300 g load added, its length is 26.5 cm. What is the extension of the rubber band?
choices: 6.5 cm
5.5 cm
quiz.rationale: Extension = length under load − original length = 26.5 − 20 = 6.5 cm. Choosing 26.5 cm confuses extension with total length, and 46.5 cm adds the two lengths instead of subtracting.
quiz.placement: Observe: structured stretching investigation (calculating the Extension column of the results table)

quiz.prompt: A 20 cm piece of sisal twine is loaded with 300 g and stretches. After the mass is removed, the twine measures 22 cm. Which statement is correct?
choices: The twine is still elastic, because it stretched when the load was added.
The twine returned to its original length, so it is elastic.
The measurement must be wrong, because materials always return to 20 cm.
The twine has been permanently deformed, so the load was beyond its elastic limit.
quiz.rationale: A material that does not return to its original length after the load is removed has been permanently deformed. This means its elastic limit was passed. Stretching alone does not show elastic behaviour.
quiz.placement: Observe: structured stretching investigation, 'Length After Load Removed' and 'Returned to Original? (Y/N)' columns

quiz.prompt: A group tests a 20 cm copper wire. After 100 g and after 200 g it returned to 20 cm once the mass was removed. After 300 g it stayed at 20.8 cm, and after 400 g and 500 g it stayed longer still. At which load should the group mark the row with a ★ (the load where the wire STOPPED returning to its original length)?
quiz.rationale: The ★ marks the first load at which the material did not return to its original length. The wire was still returning after 200 g and first failed to return at 300 g, so the elastic limit lies between 200 g and 300 g.
quiz.placement: Observe: key observation prompt, 'At what load did the material STOP returning to its original length? Mark this row with a ★'

quiz.prompt: A learner says: 'A material is elastic if it stretches a lot.' A thin copper wire stretched a little and stayed longer after the load was removed. Which is the best correction of the learner's idea?
choices: Elasticity means the material does not stretch at all when a force is applied.
Elasticity is the ability to return to the original shape and size after the deforming force is removed, however much the material stretched.
Elasticity means the material breaks easily when stretched.
Elasticity means the material stays permanently stretched after the force is removed.
quiz.rationale: Elasticity is about returning to the original shape and size, not about how far a material stretches. Copper wire stretched but did not return, so it is not behaving elastically.
quiz.placement: Explain: Step 3, formalising the definitions of ELASTICITY and PLASTIC BEHAVIOUR on the board

quiz.prompt: In a CER (Claim–Evidence–Reasoning) statement about sisal twine, which sentence is EVIDENCE?
choices: The sisal twine is plastic.
Plastic materials are permanently deformed after a force is removed.
When 300 g was added, the extension was 2.0 cm, and after the load was removed the twine did not return to 20 cm.
This means the twine passed its elastic limit, so it cannot return to its original shape.
quiz.rationale: Evidence is what was measured or observed: the load, the extension and whether the twine returned. 'The twine is plastic' is the claim, and the other two sentences are reasoning or a definition.
quiz.placement: Explain: Step 2, individual CER statement in the science journal

quiz.prompt: A thin copper wire is bent by hand and stays bent when released. Which particle-level description best explains this?
choices: The particles are destroyed when the wire is bent.
The particles return to their original positions, but the bonds disappear.
The particles move apart and then spring back to their original positions.
The particles shift to new positions permanently and are held there by new bonds.
quiz.rationale: In plastic deformation, particles move past one another to new positions and are held there by new bonds, so the change stays after the force is removed. Particles that spring back would mean elastic behaviour.
quiz.placement: Model Building: Panel B, plastic material (copper wire under load, then released)

quiz.prompt: Two ropes on a footbridge are made of sisal. Under the same load, the old rope stretches and then snaps without returning to its original length. Which statement best describes the old rope's behaviour?
choices: It behaved elastically, because it is made of a natural fibre.
It behaved plastically, because plastic materials always stretch less than elastic ones.
It behaved plastically, because it was permanently deformed beyond its elastic limit before it snapped.
It behaved elastically, because it stretched a lot.
quiz.rationale: The old rope did not return to its original length, which is permanent (plastic) deformation beyond the elastic limit. Stretching a lot does not make a material elastic, and the fibre type does not decide this.
quiz.placement: Model Building: connecting sentence 'The old sisal rope behaved like Panel ___ because…' and the Explain-phase question about the OLD Kericho rope

lessons.title: Elastic Potential Energy and the Elastic Limit: How Much Can a Material Store Before It Fails?

quiz.prompt: A rubber band is stretched and held. Where is the energy stored while it is stretched?
choices: In the hand that is pulling it
Nowhere, because the rubber band is not moving
In the stretched rubber band itself, as elastic potential energy
In the force being applied to it
quiz.rationale: Energy is stored in the stretched material itself as elastic potential energy. It is not in the hand or in the force, and it is released when the band springs back.
quiz.placement: Predict: 'Where was the energy while the rubber band was stretched?' (Think-Pair-Share)

quiz.prompt: On a graph of force (in newtons) against extension (in metres) for a spring, what does the area under the straight-line part of the graph represent?
choices: The energy stored in the spring, in joules
The safe working load, in newtons
The elastic limit, in metres
The spring constant k, in N per m
quiz.rationale: Newtons multiplied by metres gives joules, so the area under a force-extension graph is the energy stored. The spring constant is the gradient, not the area.
quiz.placement: Observe: teacher shades the triangle under the linear region of the projected force-extension graph and writes AREA = ENERGY

quiz.prompt: An older rope sample is pulled by a test force of 2 N and stretches by 0.08 m. The force-extension graph is a straight line, so the area under it is a triangle. How much energy is stored in the rope?
quiz.rationale: The area is a triangle, so energy = ½ × base × height = ½ × 2 N × 0.08 m = 0.08 J. Using F × x without the half gives 0.16 J, which wrongly treats the area as a rectangle.
quiz.placement: Observe: data card calculation of the triangle area for the older rope (2 N test force, x = 0.08 m)

quiz.prompt: A matatu suspension spring has a spring constant k = 18 000 N per m. At full load it is compressed by 0.30 m. Using Ep = ½kx², how much elastic potential energy is stored in the spring?
quiz.rationale: Ep = ½ × 18 000 × (0.30)² = ½ × 18 000 × 0.09 = 810 J. Forgetting to square x gives 2 700 J, and leaving out the half gives 1 620 J.
quiz.placement: Explain Task 2: Kenyan worked example A (matatu suspension spring), part (a)

quiz.prompt: A matatu suspension spring reaches its elastic limit when it is compressed by 0.35 m. At full load with 8 passengers it is compressed by 0.30 m. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The spring is unsafe because the load is very heavy
The spring has passed its elastic limit and will be permanently deformed
Nothing can be concluded without knowing the mass of the matatu
The spring is operating within its elastic limit, so it is safe and will recover
quiz.rationale: A compression of 0.30 m is less than the 0.35 m elastic limit. The spring is still in the region where it recovers, so it is operating safely.
quiz.placement: Explain Task 2: Kenyan worked example A, part (b) (comparing extension with the elastic limit)

quiz.prompt: A bungee cord at an adventure park has k = 120 N per m. At the lowest point of a jump the cord is stretched by 8.0 m. How much elastic potential energy is stored in the cord at that point?
quiz.rationale: Ep = ½ × 120 × (8.0)² = ½ × 120 × 64 = 3 840 J. Leaving out the half gives 7 680 J, and not squaring x gives 480 J.
quiz.placement: Explain Task 3: Kenyan worked example B (bungee cord at a Nairobi adventure park)

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly defines the safe working load of a material?
choices: The maximum load the material can bear while staying within its elastic limit, so it recovers afterwards
The weight of the material itself
The load at which the material finally snaps
The load that stores the greatest possible energy, whatever happens to the material
quiz.rationale: Safe working load is the maximum load that keeps the material within its elastic limit, where Hooke's Law holds and the material recovers. The breaking load is higher, not the same thing.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher formally introduces 'safe working load' and learners write the definition in their notebooks

quiz.prompt: A farmer's older sisal rope stretched and then snapped when an 80 kg sack of tea leaves was placed on a footbridge. A newer rope of similar appearance survived the same load. Which explanation is best?
choices: The older rope obeyed Hooke's Law all the way to snapping, so it could not fail
The older rope had a higher safe working load than the new rope, so it stored less energy
The energy was stored in the sack rather than in the rope, so the rope snapped
The load was beyond the older rope's safe working load, so it went past its elastic limit and was permanently deformed until it failed
quiz.rationale: The older rope had a lower elastic limit and a lower safe working load. The sack's load exceeded it, so the rope passed its elastic limit, deformed permanently and failed.
quiz.placement: Model Building: annotated force-extension graph of the two Kericho ropes and the one-paragraph causal explanation

lessons.title: Hooke's Law — Measuring Spring Constant and Finding the Elastic Limit

quiz.prompt: A steel spring stretches by 4 cm when a 1 N load hangs from it. The spring obeys Hooke's Law. What extension do you expect when a 4 N load hangs from the same spring?
choices: 8 cm
4 cm
16 cm
5 cm
quiz.rationale: Extension is directly proportional to force. 4 N is 4 times 1 N, so the extension is 4 × 4 cm = 16 cm. An answer of 8 cm comes from doubling instead of quadrupling.
quiz.placement: Prediction Slip: predicted extension for the 4 N load (diagram B)

quiz.prompt: A group measures the natural length of a spring as 20.0 cm. After adding a 2 N load, the spring's new length is 26.5 cm. What is the extension of the spring?
choices: 6.5 cm
quiz.rationale: Extension = new length − natural length = 26.5 − 20.0 = 6.5 cm. Recording the total length (26.5 cm) is the common error the teacher checks for in the results table.
quiz.placement: Observe: spring and slotted masses investigation, results table (Force (N) | Extension (cm))

quiz.prompt: When reading the length of a spring against a metre rule, why should your eye be level with the bottom of the spring coil?
choices: To make the load heavier
To avoid parallax error in the reading
To make the spring stop stretching
To increase the spring constant
quiz.rationale: Reading from above or below the mark gives a wrong value because of parallax error. Keeping the eye level with the coil gives an accurate length.
quiz.placement: Observe: teacher demonstration of the setup at the front bench (reading the ruler)

quiz.prompt: In a Hooke's Law investigation, a steel spring is stretched by 0.12 m when a 3 N force is applied. It is still within its elastic limit. What is the spring constant k?
choices: 25 N/m
4 N/m
36 N/m
quiz.rationale: k = F ÷ x = 3 N ÷ 0.12 m = 25 N/m. Using 12 cm without converting to metres gives 0.25 N/m, which is wrong.
quiz.placement: Explain: calculating k from the force-extension graph and the F/x ratio check

quiz.prompt: A spring has a spring constant k = 20 N/m. A force of 5 N is applied to it, within its elastic limit. What is the extension of the spring?
choices: 4 m
quiz.rationale: Using F = kx, x = F ÷ k = 5 N ÷ 20 N/m = 0.25 m. Multiplying F by k gives 100, and inverting the ratio gives 4; both are wrong.
quiz.placement: Explain: worked example using F = kx (spring with k = 20 N/m)

quiz.prompt: A spring is loaded with more and more mass until the force-extension graph starts to curve away from a straight line. What does this point on the graph tell you about the spring?
choices: The spring has become full and will not stretch any more
The spring constant k has doubled
The spring has returned to its natural length
The spring has reached its elastic limit, and beyond it the spring will not return to its natural length
quiz.rationale: The point where the graph curves away from linearity marks the elastic limit. Beyond it the spring is permanently deformed and stays longer than its natural length. The spring keeps stretching; it does not stop.
quiz.placement: Explain: introducing the elastic limit and annotating graphs (revisiting the prediction slips)

quiz.prompt: Two ropes of similar appearance carry the same heavy load. One rope returns to its original length. The other stretches and then snaps. Using what you learnt about springs, which statement is the best explanation for the rope that snapped?
choices: It probably had a lower spring constant k and a lower elastic limit, so the load took it past its elastic limit into permanent deformation
It had a higher elastic limit than the other rope, so it deformed permanently
The ropes look alike, so they must have the same k and the same elastic limit
Elastic limit has nothing to do with whether a rope snaps
quiz.rationale: A material with a lower k and a lower elastic limit is more likely to be taken past its elastic limit by the same load. This leads to permanent deformation and failure. Looks alone do not tell us a material's k or elastic limit.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: PARTIAL ANSWER linking k and elastic limit to the Kericho rope that snapped

quiz.prompt: A sack of tea leaves has a mass of 80 kg. Taking g = 10 N/kg, what is the downward force (weight) the sack exerts on a bridge rope?
choices: 8 N
quiz.rationale: Weight = mass × g = 80 kg × 10 N/kg = 800 N. This is the force drawn as the vertical dashed line on the rope force-extension graphs.
quiz.placement: Model Building: Rope Model revision, dashed line at F = 80 kg × 10 m/s² on the force-extension graphs

lessons.title: Stress, Strain, and the Young's Modulus: Predicting Which Rope Will Snap

quiz.prompt: Two rubber strips are both 20 cm long and look the same width. One is new and the other has been left in the sun and stretched many times. A learner says, 'They look the same, so they will both snap at the same load.' What is the best way to decide which strip will snap first?
choices: Measure stress and strain for each strip and compare the stress at which each one fractures
Choose the strip that looks newer, because appearance shows strength
Pick the strip that stretches more, because stretching always means it is stronger
Assume both are equal because they have the same length and width
quiz.rationale: Appearance does not show a material's internal properties. Measuring stress and strain gives numbers (such as fracture stress) that allow a prediction before the test.
quiz.placement: Predict: two strips displayed on the retort stand (Rope A new sisal / Rope B old sisal) and the Think-Pair-Share predictions

quiz.prompt: In the Stress-Strain Investigation, a rubber strip has a width of 10 mm and a thickness of 2 mm. A mass of 120 g hangs from it. Take g = 10 N/kg. What is the stress in the strip?
quiz.placement: Step 1 and Step 2 of the Stress-Strain Investigation: calculating cross-sectional area, force F = mg and stress F/A

quiz.prompt: A rubber strip has an original length of 20 cm. After a load is added its length is 23 cm. What is the strain?
choices: 3 cm
quiz.rationale: Extension = 23 − 20 = 3 cm. Strain = ΔL/L₀ = 3/20 = 0.15. Strain is a ratio of two lengths, so it has no units.
quiz.placement: Step 2 of the Stress-Strain Investigation: calculating extension ΔL and strain (ΔL/L₀) for each load

quiz.prompt: From a stress-strain graph, a learner finds that in the linear region a material has a stress of 2.0 × 10⁶ Pa when the strain is 0.25. What is the Young's Modulus of the material?
quiz.rationale: E = stress ÷ strain = 2.0 × 10⁶ / 0.25 = 8.0 × 10⁶ Pa. E is the gradient of the linear region of the graph.
quiz.placement: Whole-class debrief: groups calculate E for Strip A and Strip B from the linear portion of their graphs

quiz.prompt: Two ropes are made of the same fibre. One is thick and one is thin. Both carry the same load. Which statement is correct?
choices: The thick rope has the larger stress and the larger E
The thin rope has the larger stress, and both ropes have the same E
The thin rope has the larger E, because it stretches more
The thick rope has the larger E, because it has more material
quiz.rationale: Stress = F/A, so the thin rope (smaller area) has the larger stress. E is a property of the material, so it is the same for both ropes because the fibre is the same.
quiz.placement: Whole-class debrief: misconception check 'a thicker rope has a higher E' (thick and thin rope, same load)

quiz.prompt: Strip B has a lower Young's Modulus than Strip A. It also has a lower fracture stress, and it snaps first under the same load. Which statement best explains why Strip B snaps first?
choices: Its lower Young's Modulus means it is stronger, so it snaps first
Its lower Young's Modulus means it is harder, so it snaps first
Its fracture stress is lower, so it breaks at a smaller stress than Strip A
Its strain has units, so it breaks sooner
quiz.rationale: Fracture stress tells how much stress a material can take before it breaks. Young's Modulus only measures stiffness (how much stress is needed for a given strain). Stiffness and strength are separate properties.
quiz.placement: Whole-class debrief: CER discussion linking E-values and fracture stress to the Kericho bridge rope

quiz.prompt: In a scratch test, a nail scratches aluminium and chalk. Aluminium scratches chalk but cannot scratch the nail. Chalk cannot scratch either of the others. Which list ranks the samples from softest to hardest?
choices: Chalk, aluminium, nail
Nail, aluminium, chalk
Aluminium, chalk, nail
Chalk, nail, aluminium
quiz.rationale: A sample that scratches another is harder than it. Chalk is scratched by both others, so it is softest. Aluminium is scratched only by the nail, so it is in the middle. The nail is scratched by none, so it is hardest.
quiz.placement: Hardness scratch test: 'who scratches whom' table and ranking from softest to hardest

quiz.prompt: An 80 kg sack of tea leaves hangs from one rope with a diameter of 10 mm. Take g = 10 N/kg and use A = πr². Which value is the stress in the rope?
quiz.placement: Model Building: adding the quantitative layer, the stress on the rope from the 80 kg tea-leaf sack

lessons.title: Final Explanation: Elastic Potential Energy, Elastic Limits, and Choosing the Right Material for a Safe Structure

quiz.prompt: A model old rope has spring constant k = 210 N/m and its elastic limit is at an extension of 2.1 m. The largest force it can carry elastically is 441 N. A heavy sack pulls on this rope with a force of 784 N. Which prediction is best supported by this data?
choices: The rope is safe, because its elastic limit extension of 2.1 m is larger than the 0.92 m extension of the new rope.
The rope was pushed beyond its elastic limit, so it will be permanently deformed and may snap.
The rope will stretch more than the new rope, so it must be the stronger rope and will survive.
The rope will return to its original length, because all ropes obey Hooke's Law whatever the load.
quiz.rationale: 784 N is about 1.8 times the 441 N the old rope can carry elastically, so the load exceeds its elastic limit and permanent deformation is expected. Stretching more does not mean stronger, and the extensions of two different ropes cannot be compared this way.
quiz.placement: Predict: refined prediction on the Kericho bridge rope data card (which rope was pushed beyond its elastic limit)

quiz.prompt: A model new rope has spring constant k = 850 N/m. A load of 784 N hangs from it and the rope obeys Hooke's Law. What is its extension?
quiz.rationale: Using Hooke's Law, x = F/k = 784 ÷ 850 ≈ 0.92 m. Dividing k by F gives 1.08 m, and multiplying F by k is not Hooke's Law.
quiz.placement: Observe, Task 2: calculating the extension of rope A under the 784 N load using x = F/k

quiz.prompt: A model rope has spring constant k = 850 N/m and is stretched by an extension x = 0.92 m. Using Ep = ½kx², how much elastic potential energy is stored in it?
quiz.rationale: Ep = ½kx² = ½ × 850 × 0.92² ≈ 360 J. Leaving out the square on x gives 391 J, and using the force value 784 as the energy is a common slip.
quiz.placement: Observe, Task 2: stored energy Ep = ½kx² for rope A

quiz.prompt: A student stretches a spring that obeys Hooke's Law by different extensions x and calculates the elastic potential energy Ep = ½kx² each time. What shape is the graph of Ep (vertical axis) against x (horizontal axis)?
choices: A straight line through the origin, because force is proportional to extension
A curve that gets steeper and steeper (a parabola), because Ep depends on x²
A curve that slopes downwards, because the spring loses energy as it stretches
A horizontal straight line, because the spring constant k stays the same
quiz.rationale: Since Ep = ½kx², Ep increases with the square of x, so the graph is a parabola that gets steeper. Only the force-extension graph (F = kx) is a straight line.
quiz.placement: Observe, Task 1: plotting Ep against x from the Lesson 4 spring data

quiz.prompt: For a rope with k = 210 N/m, Hooke's Law would give an extension of 784 ÷ 210 = 3.73 m under a 784 N load. However, the rope's elastic limit is at an extension of 2.1 m (a force of 441 N). Why is 3.73 m not a trustworthy measurement of the rope's extension?
choices: Hooke's Law does not work for ropes made of natural fibre at any load.
The rope would stretch less than 3.73 m because heavier loads make ropes stiffer.
The calculation is wrong because k should be divided by the force instead.
Hooke's Law only holds up to the elastic limit, and 784 N is beyond it, so force and extension are no longer proportional.
quiz.rationale: Hooke's Law applies only within the elastic limit. Beyond it the rope is permanently deformed, so 3.73 m only shows what a rope that kept obeying Hooke's Law would do.
quiz.placement: Observe, Task 3: comparing 784 N with the 441 N at rope B's elastic limit

quiz.prompt: A matatu suspension spring has k = 12 000 N/m. When four passengers board, the spring is compressed by x = 0.23 m. Using Ep = ½kx², how much elastic potential energy is stored in the spring?
quiz.rationale: Ep = ½kx² = ½ × 12 000 × 0.23² ≈ 317 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 635 J, and forgetting to square x gives 1380 J.
quiz.placement: Explain, Worked Example 1: matatu suspension spring on Thika Road, part (b)

quiz.prompt: A person of mass 65 kg jumps from a platform on a bungee cord and falls 20 m to the lowest point, where they are momentarily at rest. Take g = 9.8 N/kg. The gravitational potential energy lost equals the energy now stored in the cord. How much energy is stored in the cord?
quiz.rationale: Energy lost = mgh = 65 × 9.8 × 20 = 12 740 J. The whole 20 m fall counts, not only the 10 m the cord stretches, so using 10 m (6370 J) is wrong.
quiz.placement: Explain, Worked Example 2: bungee cord at a Nairobi adventure park on Ngong Road, part (a)

quiz.prompt: On a force-extension graph for a rope, what does the elastic limit mark?
choices: The start of the graph, where the extension is zero
The point where the rope breaks into two pieces
The point where the rope stores no energy
The largest force or extension beyond which the rope is permanently deformed
quiz.rationale: The elastic limit is the 'point of no return': beyond it the material does not return to its original shape. Breaking happens later, at the breaking point.
quiz.placement: Explain: board diagram of the force-extension graph (Hooke's Law region, elastic limit, plastic deformation, breaking point)

quiz.prompt: A farmer wants a rope for a bridge that must safely carry a 784 N load again and again. Rope A has k = 850 N/m with an elastic limit at an extension of 1.5 m. Rope B has k = 210 N/m with an elastic limit at an extension of 2.1 m. Which recommendation is best?
choices: Rope B, because its elastic limit extension of 2.1 m is larger, so it is the stronger rope.
Rope B, because it has the smaller spring constant and so stretches more before snapping.
Rope A, because the largest force it can carry elastically is about 1275 N, which is above 784 N.
Either rope, because both obey Hooke's Law so both can carry any load safely.
quiz.rationale: Rope A's elastic-limit force is F = kx = 850 × 1.5 = 1275 N, above 784 N, so it stays elastic. Rope B's is only 210 × 2.1 = 441 N, so 784 N would deform it permanently.
quiz.placement: Model: Final Explanation letter to the Kericho Farmer (material recommendation and safe working load)
